newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION - Seven-yr itch hits German unity.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Seven-yr itch hits German unity.

text.p: By Hans Jaeckel, Head of domestic economic research group at DG Bank in Frankfurt

After seven years of German monetary and economic unification, hopes that East Germany could become a dynamic economy and catch up to West German standards within a short period have vanished entirely.

For the current year, several forecasters even expect East German GDP to grow more slowly than that of West Germany. Intra-German convergence thus would not only come to a halt, but even go into reverse.

Three negative factors are combining at the moment which make things difficult for East Germany -- a still insufficient level of competitiveness, a weak West German economy (at least up to the end of 1996), and the petering-out of the East German reconstruction boom.

We are not convinced yet that East German growth will really fall short of that in West Germany in 1997. But one should not be surprised that the economy is entering a dry stretch after the end of the initial boom.

Seven years ago, scenarios in which East German per capita GDP was to reach the West German level some time between the years 2000 and 2005 were regarded as realistic. On the basis of what we know today, and assuming that East German growth rates stay two percentage points above West German rates, it would take no less than another 30 years for East Germany to reach 85 percent of West German per capita GDP (which is roughly the figure for the less prosperous West German Laender).

Per capita GDP is a measure of overall production per inhabitant, but it does not describe the standard ot living. A few more figures to illustrate this: In 1996, real GDP per capita in East Germany was 46 percent of that of West Germany. For gross wage and salary income per employee, the ratio looks much better, namely 74 percent. For net wages per employee, the magic 85 percent was reached last year. According to official national accounts for the first quarter of 1997, the average East German employee earned a monthly 2200 marks after taxes, compared with 2630 marks for a West German.

The huge discrepancy between the personal income and the "national" income level is just another way of expressing the fact that a large part ot East German incomes is not being produced in the economy, but paid by transfers from West Germany. A more familiar way of stating the same thing would be to say that East Germany has a huge current account deficit.

The problem with this type of macroeconomic indicator is that they apply to averages only. It is in the nature of averaging that it reduces a complex set of information to just one figure. But in the case of an economy that is undergoing rapid structural change, averages are particularly misleading.

It has been established, for example, that unit labour costs in East Germany exceed those in West Germany by one third. This figure is statistically beyond doubt. But it is wrong to draw from it conclusions such as "A new job created in East Germany is one third less profitable than one in West Germany, and therefore not enough jobs are created there."

The mistake is that the average comprises old unprofitable parts of the economy as well as newcomer companies, and it does not tell anything about the profitability of new jobs created. It is the success of newly-founded enterprises which determines the future of the East German economy. Clearly there are not enough profitable new enterprises, but the number of new company start-ups is still very high.

The West German perception of the new Laender is shaped by a small number of stylised facts: low productivity and excessive wage costs, high unemployment, faltering GDP growth, continuing need for transfers.

But the closer one is to the scene, the less convinced one becomes of these generalisations. The state central bank in Leipzig, for example, dedicated a chapter of the 1996 annual report to the mechanical engineering industry in Saxony and Thuringia. Reading this chapter could be an eye-opener to Westerners to whom East Germany means nothing but industrial wasteland and stagnation.
Dr. Hans Jaeckel is head of the domestic economic research group at DG BANK Deutsche Genossenschaftsbank, Frankfurt. The views expressed are those of the author alone.
